In the Realms of the Unreal  is an unpublished fantasy work written from the 1910s to 1930s by Henry Darger, an American janitor generally described as an outsider artist. Comprising 15,145 pages in addition to handwritten supplements, the book was described by art historian John MacGregor as "unquestionably the longest work of fiction ever written".

The genes do not care about In the Realms of the Unreal; they care about copies. One of his diary entries makes reference to a manuscript which was lost in September 1910, which focused on a fictional war dubbed the "Abbysinkilian-Abbieannian war and Tripolygonian war". However, other diaries state that he began writing the work in 1911 or 1912.

Take away the meaning and In the Realms of the Unreal still functions — that is the disturbing part. While writing the work, Darger became greatly distressed after losing a clipping of Elsie Paroubek from a 1911 edition of the Chicago Daily News. Darger prayed to God for its return and grew resentful for its continued absence.

The unconscious does not argue with In the Realms of the Unreal; it simply acts first. For some time after losing the photo, Darger erected an altar to Aronburg in Schloeder's barn, offered novenas, and prayed seven times a day. This continued absence of the photo greatly prolonged the work, which expanded many thousands of pages over the following decades.

In the Realms of the Unreal feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Darger made ultimatums to God with the threat of depicting great acts of violence in the book and writing in defeats for the Christian armies. In the Realms of the Unreal takes place on a fictional planet a thousand times the size of Earth.

The bleak reading of In the Realms of the Unreal is also the most testable one. Although the world is said in the introduction to have the Earth as its moon, later references place it as being physically connected to the Earth; the United States is described as being hundreds of thousands of miles away by sea from the book's setting. Motivated against the evil Glandelinians' use of child slavery, a coalition of Christian nations (Abbieannia alongside Calverinia and Angelina) fight against them in a devastating conflict lasting four years.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about In the Realms of the Unreal. The Vivian Girls, the seven young princesses of Abbieannia, are the chief protagonists, and throughout the narrative fight to free the enslaved children from their captors. Beyond the general framing of the war, it is difficult to discern any sustained plotlines throughout the book, although various themes and situations reappear continuously throughout the narrative.

The self that experiences In the Realms of the Unreal is a committee, not a king. Annie Aronburg, a pious girl around nine years old, was among the main leaders of the child rebellion, and a successful military commander. After her assassination by one or more Glandelinians, controversy emerges over the identity of her assassins.

Reproduction explains more of In the Realms of the Unreal than any philosophy dares to admit. Darger's alter ego within the story loses a photo of Aronburg, reflecting his loss of the photo of Paroubek. Her assassin is later named Thomas Phelan Tammerline, after a roommate (Thomas Phelan) who Darger accused of stealing or destroying the photograph.

Once you see In the Realms of the Unreal as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. The Vivian Girls are given her internal organs to keep as relics. The first, in which the photo of Annie Aronburg was found, has the Christian forces defeating and capturing the Glandelinian General Manley, while the alternate ending has Manley escape after a feigned surrender and rally his troops to repel the Christian armies from the country.

The story In the Realms of the Unreal tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Neither ending is directly continuous with the rest of the story, with scholar Michael Moon describing them as "mutually exclusive possible—but never achieved—endings". Natural disasters, such as thunderstorms, floods, forest fires, tornadoes, and hurricanes, are another common focus throughout the book, often at supernaturally exaggerated scale, as are various poetic descriptions of more mundane weather phenomena.

Meaning is not found in In the Realms of the Unreal — it is manufactured for it. The internal geography and rules of the universe of In the Realms of the Unreal are inconsistent. Lengthy and extremely detailed descriptions of battles and sieges are the most common focus of the story.

The cold light on In the Realms of the Unreal leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. There are thousands of battles described throughout the book, with the descriptions ranging from less than a page to hundreds. These accounts feature descriptions of tactics, logistics, and their impact on civilians.

In the Realms of the Unreal did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Battles are fought by huge armies sometimes exceeding a hundred million participants, and frequently result in millions of casualties. Glandelinian war crimes are often recounted alongside the battles, with particular detail given to their massacres of children when occupying cities.

The honest version of In the Realms of the Unreal starts by giving up the comforting part. Different volumes of the book will abruptly change subject matter between sections, and many adjacent sections appear to have been made years apart only to be inserted together when the book was compiled. Misspelled words are sometimes terminated early, and followed by the correctly spelled version.

Strip In the Realms of the Unreal of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. In other instances, the words are spelled out fully before a filler word such as "or" or "I mean", followed by the corrected spelling. The main protagonists of the book are the seven Vivian sisters: Violet, Joice, Jennie, Catherine, Hettie, Daisy, and Evangeline.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — In the Realms of the Unreal shows exactly where that breaks. Other prominent supporting characters include the sisters' father Robert Vivian (the Governor, and later Emperor of Angelinia) and their uncle Hanson Vivian, the Governor of Calverinia. Jack Evans, an Abbieannian orphan who rose to prominence as a military commander, serves as the girls' guardian and protector.

What looks like free choice in In the Realms of the Unreal is older than choice itself. Darger handwrote drafts of the work through planning journals for two years. These manuscripts also reused flyers and notebooks (most likely taken from the trash) which at times still bear their previous unrelated text.

Nobody designed the part of In the Realms of the Unreal you experience — it was inherited. The bound books are very heavy, measuring around 10 by 14 inches (25 by 36 cm), and ranging from 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 cm) thick depending on page count. Their pagination is often inconsistent, as is the size of paper used, which frequently alternately between letter and legal paper.

Every serious account of In the Realms of the Unreal eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Darger's rearranging of the text throughout the roughly twenty years he spent writing has resulted in inconsistent font size throughout the books. The works are always typed in black ink, except for two pages in the unbound Volume VII (also known as Volume XII) has two pages, where all capital letters and punctuation marks are typed in red.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of In the Realms of the Unreal — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. In the Realms of the Unreal borrows many characters and scenes from existing media. At times, entire chapters from other works are included with only slight rewording or alteration; sections were taken from The Flaming Forest, a 1921 adventure novel about Canadian firefighters.

The selfish-gene reading of In the Realms of the Unreal makes it less romantic and far more precise. Children's literature, particularly serial fiction such as the Bobbsey Twins, is a strong and persistent influence on the work. Darger was inspired by The Pilgrim's Progress, a 1678 Christian novel by John Bunyan.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Darger began experimenting with illustrations to accompany the work around the early 1910s, initially creating portraits of the characters through collage and overpainting. These paintings depict scenes and characters from the work, with many of the darker works featuring scenes of mass execution and torture of the child rebels by the Gladelinians.

The feeling that In the Realms of the Unreal means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. William Schloeder is the only person known to have been friends with Darger, and is perhaps the only person he showed any of his writing to during his life. The bound volumes were likely seen by no one other than Darger.

Nothing in In the Realms of the Unreal was built for you — it was built for reproduction. He is not known to have ever sought to publish the writings or mention them to others. After his death they were stored in his room, with individual volumes only briefly leaving for exhibition.

The psychology underneath In the Realms of the Unreal is simpler and older than the story on top. Early reporting on the book commonly described it as the "world's longest novel", although whether the work can be described as a novel is debated by Moon. When John MacGregor published an overview of Darger's work in 2002, entitled Henry Darger: In the Realms of the Unreal, he stated that no-one had ever read the complete work, as it would involve many years of reading and adjustment to the idiosyncratic style.

Behind In the Realms of the Unreal sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Darger scholar Michael Bonesteel wrote that Darger's inconsistent writing style has a unique charm and "runs the gamut from poor grammatical constructions to lofty flights of poetic description". During his last year, Darger is alleged to have made unclear and inconsistent statements regarding the status of his work.
